item.title: 1,755 Billion Dollars Short
item.dc:creator: Pawan
item.description:
Line up eight years of India’s merchandise trade data, at the 8-digit tariff-line level — 11,993 distinct export codes, 11,551 import codes, close to 4 million monthly observations — and one number sits at the bottom of every table: a cumulative trade deficit of USD 1,755.4 billion between April 2018 and March 2026. Exports of USD 3,130.1 billion against imports of USD 4,885.5 billion. Every single year in the dataset closed in deficit. Not most years. Every year.

That kind of consistency should change how the number gets talked about. A deficit that shows up once in a while is a cyclical story — currency movements, a bad commodity year, a one-off import surge. A deficit that shows up in eight consecutive years, through a pandemic, a war, and a domestic manufacturing push, is not cyclical. It’s the shape of the Indian economy — and it echoes a finding from a decade-old structural-break analysis of India’s exports and imports, which found no stable long-run equilibrium relationship between the two series across six decades of Indian trade history, meaning the deficit does not simply self-correct through the channels standard trade theory would predict (structural-break cointegration study, North American Journal of Economics and Finance).

The two commodities that explain almost everything

Look past the aggregate numbers and the deficit resolves into something much simpler than “structural imbalance” implies: it is, to a striking degree, an oil story with a gold problem attached.

Crude petroleum alone accounts for USD 559.1 billion of cumulative imports over the eight-year window — the single largest import line by a wide margin — with refined petroleum products (USD 411.0 billion) close behind. Add gold (USD 285.9 billion) and rough diamonds (USD 112.1 billion), and four commodity lines account for a meaningful share of India’s entire eight-year import bill.

On the export side, the same commodity — petroleum — shows up again, but reversed. Refined diesel (USD 131.5 billion), petrol (USD 62.0 billion), aviation turbine fuel (USD 56.7 billion), and other refined products together make petroleum India’s largest export category too, because Jamnagar and India’s other mega-refineries buy crude, process it, and re-export the output at a margin. India imports the raw material for its top export.

HS Chapter Description Exports (USD B) Imports (USD B)
27 Mineral Fuels 500.9 1,527.5
71 Gems & Precious Stones 276.9 604.9
85 Electrical Machinery 216.3 544.0
84 Machinery 212.6 422.1
30 Pharmaceuticals 160.6 —
29 Organic Chemicals 158.3 199.5

The rule of thumb buried in this table: a USD 10 per barrel move in crude prices shifts India’s annual trade balance by roughly USD 15–18 billion, in either direction, more or less automatically — before a single policy decision gets made.

What “concentration” actually looks like, numerically

Trade economists measure how spread-out (or bunched-up) a country’s trade basket is using the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index — the same tool used to measure market power in antitrust cases, repurposed here to measure commodity concentration. A score under 1,000 signals a diversified basket; above 2,500 signals dangerous concentration in a handful of goods.

India’s export HHI sits at 569 — genuinely diversified, helped by the fact that petroleum’s dominance is offset by sizeable pharmaceutical, engineering, and gems exports sitting underneath it. India’s import HHI sits at 1,390 — noticeably more concentrated, driven by the same three culprits repeatedly: crude oil, electronics, and gold. India’s import basket, in other words, has fewer places to hide from a shock than its export basket does — consistent with bilateral-trade research showing India runs deficits with nine of its ten largest trading partners simultaneously, a pattern that recurring studies attribute less to any single bilateral relationship than to exactly this kind of concentrated import dependence (bilateral trade performance research, 2026).

The three-phase story hiding inside “eight years of deficit”

Zoom into the year-by-year numbers and the deficit isn’t a flat, unchanging feature — it moves through three distinct regimes.

Year Exports (USD B) Imports (USD B) Balance (USD B)
2018 324.8 514.5 −189.7
2019 324.3 485.9 −161.6
2020 276.5 373.3 −96.8
2021 395.5 573.2 −177.7
2022 453.2 720.2 −267.0
2023 431.4 673.7 −242.3
2024 442.8 718.2 −275.4
2025 445.1 755.3 −310.2

Phase one, the contraction: 2019–20, when both flows collapsed roughly 22% as COVID lockdowns shut down global demand and supply chains simultaneously — and, paradoxically, this is the year with the smallest deficit in the dataset, at USD 96.8 billion, purely because imports fell faster than exports did.

Phase two, the expansion: 2021–22, a V-shaped recovery so sharp that exports hit an all-time high of USD 453.2 billion in 2022, driven by a global commodity super-cycle and pent-up post-pandemic demand. The deficit widened sharply in the same window, because imports rebounded even faster.

Phase three, the plateau-with-a-widening-gap: 2023 onward, where exports have essentially flatlined in the USD 430–450 billion range for three consecutive years while imports kept climbing, pushing the deficit to a dataset record of USD 310.2 billion in 2025 — nearly triple the 2020 trough.

That third phase is the one that should worry policymakers more than the first two. A deficit that widens because a shock temporarily distorts trade flows is self-correcting. A deficit that widens because exports have stopped growing while imports keep growing is not.

Diversification is real — but it’s a rounding error next to petroleum

It would be unfair to the data to say nothing is changing on the export side. Pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, electronic components, and agricultural products have all genuinely expanded their share of the export basket over the eight-year window, and India’s export HHI has drifted marginally lower as a result. Basmati rice alone brought in USD 34.5 billion cumulatively — a top-ten export commodity in its own right, and a reminder that agricultural trade is not a footnote in this dataset.

But scale it against the numbers above: the top five HS chapters still account for over 60% of total exports. Diversification is happening at the margin, not at the core. The core is still petroleum, gems, and machinery, exactly as it was in 2018.

The import line that’s actually new

If there’s a genuinely fresh structural pressure in this dataset — something that wasn’t as prominent in earlier decades of India’s trade history — it’s electronics. Monolithic integrated circuits alone account for USD 75.7 billion in cumulative imports, and the electronics import bill overall has grown faster than any other major category across the eight years, driven simultaneously by consumer demand (smartphones, laptops) and by the assembly requirements of India’s own Production-Linked Incentive manufacturers, who import components to build finished electronics domestically. It’s an uncomfortable irony: a policy designed to reduce import dependence over the long run is, in the short run, adding to the import bill it’s meant to eventually shrink.

What the ledger says about the next decade

Three forces will determine whether India’s trade deficit narrows or keeps widening through the next cycle. The energy transition should, mechanically, reduce both crude imports and refined-product exports over time — shrinking the two biggest lines on both sides of the ledger simultaneously, a wash on the trade balance but a genuine reduction in exposure to oil-price shocks. The success (or failure) of import-substitution manufacturing in electronics and capital goods will determine whether the fastest-growing import category keeps growing. And market diversification — away from a trading system still centred on the US and China, toward partners in Africa, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia — will determine how much of any future export growth actually shows up as diversification, rather than just more of the same commodities sold to more of the same three buyers.

None of that changes the headline fact sitting at the bottom of eight years of tariff-line data: USD 1,755.4 billion of cumulative deficit, in a straight, unbroken line, through a pandemic, a war, and a manufacturing push that hasn’t yet turned the trend around.

Literature Review

The empirical literature on India’s trade deficit has a long-running methodological debate at its core: is the deficit a sustainable feature of a fast-growing, capital-importing economy, or a structural imbalance that eventually forces a reckoning? An early and still-cited contribution applying structural-break cointegration techniques to India’s exports and imports found no stable long-run equilibrium relationship between the two series across six decades — evidence, the authors argued, that India’s trade position has not historically been self-correcting through the channels standard trade theory would predict, and that policy intervention rather than automatic adjustment has done most of the work in any period of narrowing. That finding, now over a decade old, sits comfortably alongside this analysis’s own three-phase reading of the 2018–2025 data: each phase break (2020 contraction, 2021–22 expansion, 2023 plateau) tracks an external shock or policy response, not a gradual equilibrium adjustment.

A second, more policy-oriented strand of literature — including recurring bilateral-trade-performance studies — has focused on the fact that India runs deficits with nine of its ten largest trading partners simultaneously, attributing this less to any single bilateral relationship than to the commodity concentration this piece quantifies via the HHI framework: energy, gold, and increasingly electronics import dependence that no single trade agreement or partner-diversification strategy can fully offset. Where this literature remains comparatively thin is on the electronics-import paradox highlighted above — the tension between PLI-driven component imports in the short run and import-substitution goals in the long run — an area that would benefit from more granular, HS-8-digit-level research as India’s electronics manufacturing base matures.

References

  • The Sustainability of Trade Deficits in the Presence of Endogenous Structural Breaks: Evidence from the Indian Economy. North American Journal of Economics and Finance (ScienceDirect).
  • India’s Bilateral Trade Performance with Major Trading Partners. (2026). The Academic (peer-reviewed working paper).
  • India’s Trade Deficit: Increasing Fast but Still Manageable. Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations (ICRIER)-affiliated commentary.
  • Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics (DGCI&S), Ministry of Commerce & Industry — monthly 8-digit HS code export/import series.
  • Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) — trade policy and licensing data.

Data: DGCI&S / DGFT monthly 8-digit HS code series, April 2018–March 2026 (11,993 export codes, 11,551 import codes). Analysis by Pawan. A companion interactive dashboard is available here.

item.title: From 323 Units to a National Security Question
item.dc:creator: Pawan
item.description:
In the spring of 2026, as Iranian strikes and a US-led response turned the Strait of Hormuz into a genuine shipping hazard, India’s crude oil basket briefly cleared $113 a barrel — more than double where it had started the year. Oil marketing companies were absorbing losses of roughly ₹13 a litre on diesel. The rupee had already shed close to a tenth of its value against the dollar over the fiscal year. And at a public event in Secunderabad, the Prime Minister did something Indian heads of government almost never do: he stood in front of a crowd and asked citizens, directly, to stop driving their petrol cars.

It made headlines as a dramatic, of-the-moment appeal. It wasn’t, really. It was the visible tip of a trend that twenty-six years of Ministry of Road Transport and Highways registration data had been quietly building toward, one fiscal year at a time.

The number that took a quarter-century to matter

In FY2000-01, India registered 323 electric vehicles. In FY2025-26, registrations crossed roughly 25 lakh — a compound annual growth rate above 40% sustained across a quarter-century, through two recessions, a pandemic, and five changes of government. EV market share, essentially flat for the entire 2000s, crossed the 5% threshold that analysts treat as the marker of mainstream adoption in FY2022-23, and reached approximately 8.5% by the close of FY2025-26, up from 7.7% a year earlier.

That headline number understates how lopsided the Indian story is compared with the rest of the world. In Europe and the US, the EV conversation is dominated by passenger cars. In India, electric two-wheelers alone account for roughly 58% of all EV sales, and India commands more than half of global electric three-wheeler sales. These are not aspirational purchases by early adopters with driveways and home chargers. They are cost calculations made by gig-economy delivery riders, e-rickshaw operators, and small logistics fleets who do the fuel-savings math in their heads before they walk into a showroom — which is exactly why a fuel-price shock moves this market faster than it moves wealthier ones.

Six forces that had to line up

No single scheme produced a 40%-plus CAGR sustained over decades. It took several forces compounding in the same direction.

Policy layering. India’s EV incentive architecture has been built in stages: FAME-I from 2015, FAME-II from 2019 to 2024 (₹11,500 crore, supporting roughly 16.29 lakh EVs), a Production Linked Incentive scheme worth ₹26,058 crore for component manufacturing, and the current PM E-Drive scheme, which targets 2.5 million subsidised electric two-wheelers and 320,000 three-wheelers, backed by roughly $315 million in vehicle and charging-infrastructure subsidies. Choice-model research evaluating FAME’s actual counterfactual impact — rather than simply its uptake numbers — found the scheme genuinely induced incremental EV sales that would not otherwise have happened, rather than merely subsidising purchases already in the pipeline (Sheldon et al., 2019). It’s the stacking of demand-side subsidies on top of supply-side manufacturing incentives, sustained over a decade, that bent the curve — not any one of them alone.

A battery-cost collapse that happened to arrive at the right moment. Global lithium-ion battery prices have fallen more than 90% since 2010. That’s not an India story specifically, but its consequences are outsized in India because it pushes electric two- and three-wheelers past cost-parity with petrol equivalents inside a payback period an ordinary buyer can actually do the arithmetic on.

Charging infrastructure finally showing up where it’s needed. Public charging stations crossed roughly 27,000–29,000 by early-to-mid 2026, from near zero in 2019, with the PM E-Drive scheme explicitly targeting Tier-2 and Tier-3 city expansion — the geography where the next wave of buyers actually lives, and where range anxiety remains the sharpest barrier.

Legacy manufacturers finally showing up too. In electric two-wheelers, established players TVS, Bajaj, and Hero MotoCorp now control roughly 61% of the market, leaning on dealer networks and after-sales infrastructure that pure-EV startups can’t match overnight. In electric cars, the picture is actually getting more competitive rather than less: Tata Motors’ share of the electric passenger vehicle market fell from around 57% in FY2024-25 to roughly 39% in FY2025-26 as JSW MG Motor, Mahindra, and Hyundai expanded their own line-ups — a healthy sign for a market that was, until recently, close to a one-brand story.

The freight and logistics pivot. Electric goods vehicles — light, medium, and heavy trucks — grew 172% year-on-year in FY2025-26, the fastest-growing segment in the market, as e-commerce fleets converted for cost and ESG reasons and PM E-Drive incentives extended to trucks for the first time.

And then, the oil shock. A 2023 study in Energy Policy by Garg, Mishra and Sinha found that India’s crude-price elasticity is low in the short run — price signals alone don’t move behaviour fast. The 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis changed the political economy of that finding. When a Prime Minister publicly urges citizens toward EVs and public transport, the oil shock has crossed into territory no subsidy programme alone had reached: direct political urgency, applied at the top.

The number that makes this a macro story, not a green one

India spent an estimated USD 134.7 billion on crude oil imports in FY2025-26. The International Energy Agency projects EV adoption and efficiency gains will avoid roughly 480,000 barrels a day of additional oil demand by 2030 (IEA, 2025–2026) — at current prices, an annual saving in the range of USD 18 billion, more than a full year’s worth of the entire cumulative FAME programme spend, recovered in avoided imports alone.

That reframes the EV transition for anyone still filing it under “environmental policy.” At the scale India now operates, it is an import-substitution and current-account story first, and a climate story second — which may be precisely why it has survived five changes of government intact.

Three gaps that could still stall it

The trajectory looks close to inevitable from a distance, but three specific weaknesses remain exposed at close range.

Geographic mismatch. Charging infrastructure is still concentrated in metros, while the buyers with the strongest cost-of-ownership case increasingly come from smaller cities. The infrastructure needs to arrive before that cohort reaches the showroom, not after — a sequencing problem, not a capacity one.

Shallow supply chains. India’s EV growth still rests substantially on imported battery cells, with China dominating global cell manufacturing. A demand shock originating in China would expose a vulnerability structurally similar to the one that produced the Secunderabad appeal in the first place — just routed through a different chokepoint.

A financing gap that isn’t really about interest rates. Electric two- and three-wheelers are disproportionately bought by micro-entrepreneurs and gig workers whose credit profiles don’t clear conventional auto-loan underwriting. Consumer-behaviour research on Indian EV adoption consistently ranks purchase price and financing access alongside range anxiety as the dominant barriers to uptake (Rathore et al., 2024; Singh et al., 2023), even as the same literature finds environmental concern playing a comparatively minor role in actual buying decisions for this segment. Until a targeted guarantee scheme closes the financing gap, a segment of buyers who are economically rational — the fuel savings genuinely pencil out — is locked out by the banking system rather than by preference.

What the data actually settles

Twenty-six years of registration data and a sustained 40%-plus CAGR have already answered the question of whether India’s EV transition happens. What remains open, entering FY2026-27 with EV penetration near 8.5% against a 2030 government target of 30%, is whether the supporting ecosystem — the charging grid, the battery supply chain, the loan desk for a three-wheeler operator in a Tier-3 town — can move at the same speed as a market that has already made up its mind. The Strait of Hormuz crisis didn’t create that market’s momentum. It just made the cost of ignoring the remaining gaps considerably more visible, to a Prime Minister and everyone else, all at once.

Literature Review

Academic work on Indian EV adoption splits along the same supply/demand line the article traces above. On the demand side, a substantial body of consumer-behaviour research — much of it applying the Technology Acceptance Model or the Theory of Planned Behaviour to Indian survey samples — consistently identifies purchase price, charging-infrastructure availability, and range anxiety as the dominant psychological barriers, with financial incentives and perceived environmental benefit as the leading pull factors. What this literature tends to under-weight, and what the two- and three-wheeler registration data foregrounds instead, is that for the majority of India’s actual EV buyers, adoption isn’t primarily an attitudinal decision at all — it’s a fleet-economics calculation made by gig workers and small operators, closer to a total-cost-of-ownership problem than a green-consumption one.

On the supply and policy side, Sheldon, Cui and colleagues’ choice-model analysis of the FAME scheme found the subsidy programme to be genuinely effective at inducing incremental EV sales rather than merely subsidising purchases that would have happened anyway — an important empirical anchor, since counterfactual effectiveness is notoriously hard to establish for vehicle subsidies internationally. More recent 2024–2025 studies applying Fuzzy AHP and structural equation modelling to expert and consumer panels have begun disaggregating barriers by segment (two-wheeler vs. four-wheeler, Tier-1 vs. Tier-2/3 city), a useful methodological shift given how differently those segments behave in the registration data. The literature has not yet, as of this writing, produced a rigorous causal estimate of how acute fuel-price shocks — of the kind India experienced in 2026 — shift adoption in the short run; the IEA’s demand-avoidance projections remain the best available approximation, and are treated as such in this piece.

References

  • Sheldon, T. L., DeShazo, J. R., et al. (2019). Studies on FAME scheme effectiveness and counterfactual EV sales simulation, Energy Economics / related working papers.
  • Rathore, A., et al. (2024). Barriers to EV Adoption in India: A Fuzzy Analytical Hierarchy Process Study. ScienceDirect.
  • Singh, V., et al. (2023). Factors Affecting Adoption Intention of Electric Vehicles: A Cross-Cultural Study. Environment, Development and Sustainability (Springer).
  • Enablers and Disablers to Plug-in Electric Vehicle Adoption in India: Insights from a Survey of Experts. (2021). ScienceDirect.
  • The Dynamics of Electrified Vehicle Adoption: An Indian Market Analysis. (2026). ScienceDirect.
  • An Empirical Study on Electric Vehicle Adoption in India: A Step Towards a Greener Environment. (2024). ScienceDirect.
  • International Energy Agency. (2025–2026). Global EV Outlook — India country projections, oil-demand avoidance estimates.
  • Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) / NITI Aayog — Vahan and ICED registration databases.
  • JMK Research & Analytics — segment-wise EV sales tracking reports, FY2024-25 and FY2025-26.

Data: MoRTH / NITI Aayog ICED database (FY2000-01–FY2025-26); JMK Research & Analytics; International Energy Agency. Analysis by Pawan. A companion interactive dashboard is available here.

item.title: Twenty-Five Years, One Barrel at a Time
item.dc:creator: Pawan
item.description:
In mid-July 2026, Brent crude touched its highest level in nearly a month, and Indian equity markets opened lower the same morning. The proximate cause was familiar to anyone who has watched an oil chart for more than a decade: a flare-up between the United States and Iran near the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil physically passes on its way to buyers like India. It is, in one sense, an old story wearing a new date. It is also the cleanest possible illustration of a fact that a full quarter-century of Indian Crude Oil Basket data makes brutally obvious: India’s fuel bill is not really set in Delhi. It is set wherever the last tanker was most recently threatened.

The basket, explained without the jargon

Every day, the Petroleum Planning & Analysis Cell publishes a number called the Indian Crude Oil Basket — a weighted average of Oman/Dubai sour crude (the heavier, cheaper-to-trade, harder-to-refine grade that dominates India’s Gulf imports) and Brent sweet crude (the lighter international benchmark). It typically trades 2–5% below Brent itself, and since 2022 that discount has widened further because of one specific development: India began buying large volumes of sanctioned-but-discounted Russian Urals crude, at times $20–35 a barrel cheaper than the prevailing international price.

Twenty-five years of this number, laid end to end, does not describe a market finding equilibrium. It describes a market lurching from shock to shock, with brief plateaus in between.

Period Basket Price (USD/bbl) What Happened
~2000–2003 $20–30 Low, stable supply
2004–2008 $30–133 China demand boom; commodity supercycle
2009 Falls to $40 Global Financial Crisis
2010–2014 $80–110 Sustained “century oil” era
2015–2016 Falls to $30 US shale boom; OPEC supply surge
2017–2019 $50–80 Gradual recovery
Apr 2020 Near $20 COVID-19 demand collapse
2021–2022 $80–125+ Post-COVID rebound + Russia-Ukraine war
2023–2025 $70–90 Stabilisation with geopolitical risk premium
2026 Spikes above $110 US-Iran conflict, Strait of Hormuz disruption

India now imports over 85% of the crude it consumes — the world’s third-largest crude importer by volume — and that dependence has essentially tripled since 1998-99, from roughly 75,000 thousand metric tonnes a year to over 230,000. Every $10 move in the basket price adds or subtracts approximately ₹1.25 lakh crore from India’s annual import bill. There is no other single commodity price that moves India’s macroeconomy this directly, this fast.

Why cheap oil didn’t make petrol cheap in 2020

Here is the detail that most retellings of the COVID oil crash leave out. When the basket price collapsed to near $20 a barrel in April 2020 — so low that some US contracts briefly traded negative, sellers paying buyers to take oil off their hands — petrol prices at Indian pumps barely moved. The reason wasn’t refining costs or currency effects. It was policy: the government raised excise duty on petrol by ₹10 a litre and on diesel by ₹13 a litre during exactly this window, capturing the windfall from cheap global oil as tax revenue rather than passing it to consumers.

Then the mirror image happened two years later. When the basket surged past $120 a barrel after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the government cut excise duty by ₹8 a litre on petrol and ₹6 a litre on diesel in May 2022, absorbing some of the shock rather than letting it flow through to the pump.

The pattern is consistent enough to be treated as a rule rather than an anomaly: the government is the actual price-smoothing mechanism in India’s fuel market, not the international crude cycle. Dynamic daily pricing, introduced in June 2017, made the pump price mechanically follow the international benchmark day by day — and academic research on India’s pass-through mechanism had already anticipated exactly this shift, finding that transmission from global to domestic prices strengthens sharply once administered pricing gives way to market-linked formulas (Bhattacharya & Sen, 2012). What that research could not fully anticipate was how deliberately the tax lever would then be used to work against that same transmission, in both directions, whenever it suited the exchequer.

Where every rupee of your ₹103 actually goes

Break down a litre of Delhi petrol at current prices and the picture is stark:

Component ₹ per Litre Share
Base price (crude + refining + OMC margin) ~₹54 ~52%
Central Excise Duty ~₹20 ~19%
State VAT and local levies (Delhi) ~₹19 ~18%
Dealer commission ~₹4 ~4%
Freight, insurance, other ~₹6 ~6%

Roughly ₹45 of every ₹103 you pay for petrol in Delhi is tax. The crude oil itself — the thing everyone blames when prices rise — accounts for only about ₹25–30. Policy-institute research on India’s petroleum tax revenue has documented this asymmetry in detail: had the 2015–2020 fall in global crude prices been fully passed through, retail prices would have been meaningfully lower than they were; instead, much of that windfall was captured as excise revenue (ORF, 2024). This is also why petrol prices across Indian metros diverge so much despite drawing on the same refineries and the same crude: Maharashtra’s higher VAT rate keeps Mumbai consistently the most expensive of the four major metros, while Delhi’s comparatively moderate VAT has kept it the cheapest.

City 2025 (₹/L) 2022 Peak 2018 Level Rise since 2018
Delhi 103.50 ~107 ~74 +₹29.50
Mumbai 105.01 ~111 ~83 +₹22.01
Chennai 100.80 ~108 ~80 +₹20.80
Kolkata 94.77 ~114 ~80 +₹14.77

Kolkata’s numbers are the most interesting in that table: the highest 2022 peak of any metro, but the smallest cumulative rise since 2018 — evidence of a state government leaning harder on VAT relief than its peers once the acute crisis passed.

The household arithmetic

For a household with one two-wheeler commuter doing 20 km a day at roughly 40 km/litre, a ₹10 rise in petrol adds about ₹150 a month — not dramatic in isolation, but compounding. A commuter using 15 litres a month paid about ₹1,110 in 2018 at ₹74/litre; at 2025 prices of ₹103.50/litre, the same 15 litres costs ₹1,553 — an extra ₹443 a month, ₹5,310 a year, and more than ₹37,000 cumulatively across seven years, before accounting for anything else fuel prices touch indirectly: freight costs baked into vegetable prices, diesel costs baked into farming, ATF costs baked into flight fares.

The 2026 test

Which brings the story back to this year. The Strait of Hormuz tensions that pushed Brent above $110–115 in parts of 2026 are not a new category of risk — the basket has weathered the 2008 supercycle, the 2020 demand collapse, and the 2022 war-driven spike. What is new is India’s position going into this shock: a Russian crude relationship built over four years that has, at various points, supplied over a third of India’s imports at a discount, a strategic petroleum reserve programme that has matured since its early pilot phase, and — for the first time in the Basket’s 25-year history — a genuinely fast-growing electric vehicle fleet absorbing some of the marginal fuel-demand growth that would otherwise have made this shock even more expensive.

None of that insulates India from the current spike. It does mean the country is entering its latest oil shock with more shock absorbers than it had in 2008, 2014, or even 2022. Whether those absorbers are enough is now, as it has been for twenty-five years running, mostly a question of what happens in the Gulf — not in Delhi.

Literature Review

The empirical literature on India’s fuel-price pass-through has a clear before-and-after hinge point: 2010, when petrol pricing was formally deregulated (diesel followed in 2014). Bhattacharya and Sen’s foundational study on oil-price transmission found that pass-through to Indian retail prices strengthened markedly once administered pricing began giving way to market-linked formulas — precisely the mechanism this piece traces through the tax-versus-crude build-up of a Delhi litre. More recent work extends the same question to the asymmetry angle explored above: a 2022 study on diesel price reforms found India’s crude-import demand has become steadily more price- and income-inelastic over time relative to earlier estimates, consistent with the pattern this analysis documents of taxation, not crude cost, absorbing most of the swing in any given price cycle.

A parallel strand of policy-institute research — most usefully summarised in ORF’s recurring analyses of petroleum tax revenue — has quantified precisely how much of the 2015–2020 low-crude window was captured as excise revenue rather than passed to consumers, the same asymmetry this piece identifies independently from the raw price data. That literature also flags a genuine equity tension this piece does not resolve: fuel taxation is mildly regressive in incidence terms, even as it functions as a de facto carbon price — India’s implicit fuel excise tax per tonne of CO2 has been estimated to exceed comparable rates in the US and China. Whether that trade-off is being managed well, as opposed to simply being convenient for the exchequer, remains a live and under-researched question as India’s 2026 oil shock forces a fresh round of tax-versus-pass-through decisions.

References

  • Bhattacharya, K., & Sen, P. (2012). Is the Oil Price Pass-Through in India Any Different? Energy Policy.
  • Diesel Price Reforms and Asymmetric Oil Price Pass-Through to Inflation: An Indian Perspective. (2022). ScienceDirect / IIMB Management Review-affiliated study.
  • Observer Research Foundation. (2024). India’s Tax Revenue from Petroleum Products: Golden Eggs That May Kill the Goose?
  • Petroleum Planning & Analysis Cell (PPAC), Government of India — monthly Indian Crude Oil Basket and retail price bulletins.
  • Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) — retail selling price data, four-metro series.
  • U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) — historical Brent crude series.

Data: Petroleum Planning & Analysis Cell (PPAC), Indian Oil Corporation, U.S. Energy Information Administration. Analysis by Pawan. A companion interactive dashboard is available here.

item.title: The Machine That Ate India’s Cash Economy
item.dc:creator: Pawan
item.description:
On the morning of 1 July 2017, a tax reform that had taken seventeen years to negotiate — through three prime ministers, a constitutional amendment, and more state-finance-minister meetings than anyone cared to count — went live at midnight in the Central Hall of Parliament. Critics called it rushed. Small traders called it a nightmare. Eight years and 26.18 lakh crore rupees of revenue later, in a single financial year, GST has become something nobody quite predicted at launch: not just a tax, but India’s most granular, most current window into the real economy.

This is the story that eight years of collection data tells — not the political story of GST, but the economic one, told entirely in the numbers the system generates every single month.

GST’s most eloquent modern defenders, before it launched, had already sketched the trade-off it would face: Michael Keen’s work on VAT design for the IMF argued that a single-rate structure is administratively simpler and less distortionary, but that most countries — India very much included — end up trading some of that simplicity for political feasibility on sensitive goods (Keen, 2009; Keen, 2013). The Chief Economic Advisor’s own 2015 committee report on the Revenue Neutral Rate is the reference point every subsequent collection number gets measured against (Government of India, 2015), and it’s worth noting just how far actual collections have outrun those original projections.

The line that keeps climbing

Strip away the debates and the headline is simple. Gross GST collection has grown from ₹7.41 lakh crore in its first, partial year (FY2017-18) to ₹22.09 lakh crore in FY2024-25 — essentially a tripling in eight years. FY2025-26, still eleven months in as this is written, has already logged ₹26.18 lakh crore.

Fiscal Year Gross Collection YoY Growth
2017-18 ₹7.41 L Cr —
2018-19 ₹11.77 L Cr +59.0%
2019-20 ₹12.22 L Cr +3.8%
2020-21 ₹11.37 L Cr −7.0%
2021-22 ₹14.88 L Cr +30.9%
2022-23 ₹18.08 L Cr +21.5%
2023-24 ₹20.18 L Cr +11.6%
2024-25 ₹22.09 L Cr +9.4%
2025-26 (Apr–Feb) ₹26.18 L Cr +18.5%

Two things jump out. The first is the V-shape around FY2020-21 — a 7% pandemic-year contraction followed by a 30.9% rebound, the sharpest single-year swing in the dataset, and a reminder that GST collection is really just a proxy for how much India is buying, selling, and building in any given month. The second is that growth has been decelerating in percentage terms even as the absolute numbers get larger — 59% in year two, 9.4% in year eight. That’s not decline; it’s a large base doing what large bases do. A tax system covering ₹22 lakh crore cannot keep growing at the pace of one covering ₹8 lakh crore.

What October 2025 quietly did to the numbers

Anyone squinting at FY2025-26’s monthly figures will notice something odd: growth, which had been running at 9–20% for most of the year, suddenly turns negative in October, November, and December 2025 — minus 0.3%, minus 8.0%, minus 4.2% — before recovering in January.

The explanation isn’t a slowdown in the economy. It’s a policy switch. The GST Compensation Cess — the special levy on tobacco, aerated drinks, and automobiles that was supposed to fund states’ revenue guarantees for exactly five years after GST launch — finally began its scheduled wind-down in October 2025. Cess collections that had run at roughly ₹23,449 crore in October 2024 fell to ₹14,340 crore in October 2025, then to ₹8,001 crore in November and ₹8,515 crore in December. The core taxes — CGST, SGST, IGST — kept climbing through this period. The headline number just stopped reflecting it, because one of its four components was being switched off in real time.

It’s a useful lesson in reading tax data: a “decline” in gross collection and a decline in economic activity are not always the same statement.

The refund machine got faster, not just bigger

A less-discussed but genuinely striking trend sits in the refund data. Annual GST refunds grew from ₹3.21 lakh crore in FY2020-21 to ₹6.43 lakh crore in FY2024-25 — a 5.94× increase — and the refund-to-gross ratio climbed steadily from 8.4% to 11.6% over the same period.

That sounds like the tax department giving away more money, but read the other way, it’s the opposite story. IGST refunds — overwhelmingly claims from exporters filing under the Letter of Undertaking scheme — dominate the refund book. A rising refund rate alongside rising net collections means India’s export base is growing and the GSTN’s processing pipeline is keeping pace with it, rather than sitting on exporters’ working capital the way it did in the system’s chaotic early years. Compliance data backs this up directly: GSTR-3B filing compliance, a rough proxy for how functional the return-filing machinery actually is, sat at 89.2% in FY2018-19 and has held above 98.9% since FY2023-24 — a genuine turnaround from the administrative gaps the Comptroller and Auditor General’s own 2019 compliance audit had flagged in the system’s early years (CAG, 2019).

Eight crore taxpayers, and 0.5% of them carry the load

If there’s one table in the GST dataset that deserves to be printed and pinned to a wall in North Block, it’s the taxpayer-constitution breakdown. As of June 2025, India had 1.53 crore active GST registrations. Proprietorships — the corner shop, the single-owner trading firm, the neighbourhood parlour — make up 80.14% of that base. Public Limited Companies make up 0.50%.

Proprietorships contribute 13.27% of GST revenue. Public Limited Companies contribute 33.83%.

Run the leverage ratio — revenue share divided by taxpayer share — and a Public Limited Company contributes 67.7 times its population share to the tax base. A Proprietorship contributes 0.2 times its share. Public Sector Undertakings, a mere 3,475 entities, punch in at an extraordinary 469.5× leverage, contributing 9.39% of all GST revenue from 0.02% of registrants.

This is not a scandal — large, formal, capital-intensive businesses have always paid disproportionate tax everywhere in the world, and the IMF’s own periodic assessments of India’s GST have argued its multi-rate structure does more to protect low-income consumers than a single-rate alternative would (IMF, 2018). But it does put a number on something that’s often asserted impressionistically in Indian tax-policy debates: GST’s revenue base is extremely concentrated at the top of the formal economy, even though its compliance burden — filing, invoicing, e-way bills — falls on all 1.53 crore registrants roughly equally. That asymmetry is arguably the single biggest unresolved design tension in GST as it enters its ninth year.

The e-way bill is now a better GDP proxy than GDP

Buried in section 8 of the underlying dataset is a number that deserves far more attention than it gets: e-way bill generation — the digital permission slip required to move goods worth over ₹50,000 across state lines or within them — has grown 3.24× since FY2018-19, from 43.35 crore bills a year to 140.71 crore in FY2025-26 (11 months). The assessable value of goods covered has crossed ₹32.7 lakh crore.

Because e-way bills are generated in real time, at the point goods actually move, they arguably tell you what’s happening in the goods economy faster and more honestly than any survey-based indicator India publishes. When intra-state EWB growth outpaces inter-state growth, as it has in recent years, it’s a signal of shorter, more localised supply chains — plausibly linked to warehousing decentralisation under GST’s own “One Nation, One Tax” logic finally removing the incentive to route goods through fewer, larger interstate hubs.

Maharashtra’s lead is not shrinking — but the chase is getting interesting

Maharashtra alone contributes north of 21% of all state-level domestic GST — more than the bottom fifteen states combined. But the fastest-growing large states in FY2024-25 were not the usual suspects: Haryana grew 16.0% year-on-year and Delhi grew 15.9%, both comfortably outpacing Maharashtra’s own growth and reflecting the expansion of services-sector activity — IT, finance, logistics — around the National Capital Region rather than manufacturing.

Eight years in, what the ledger actually says

None of this requires anyone to have an opinion about GST as a political project. The eight-year dataset simply says: revenue has nearly tripled; compliance infrastructure that was genuinely broken in 2018-19 now works; refunds move faster; the formal, large-enterprise economy carries a wildly disproportionate share of the tax base; and a real-time logistics indicator now exists inside the tax system that didn’t exist before it. Whatever else GST turns out to have been — messy launch, contested rate structure, endless Council meetings — it has, almost as a side effect, built India one of its best pieces of high-frequency economic infrastructure. The next test, as the Compensation Cess fully sunsets through 2026, is whether the system’s next chapter is written with the same discipline as its recovery from a pandemic-year collapse.

Literature Review

GST’s academic literature divides fairly cleanly into two eras. The pre-2017 era was dominated by revenue-neutral-rate modelling — the Chief Economic Advisor’s 2015 committee report on the RNR remains the reference point, and it’s worth noting how far actual collections have outrun its original projections. International public-finance scholars writing before implementation, most influentially Michael Keen’s work on VAT design for the IMF, framed GST’s central design tension well in advance: a single-rate VAT is administratively simpler and less distortionary, but India’s multi-slab structure was always going to trade some of that simplicity for political feasibility and revenue protection on sensitive goods. The dataset examined here is, in a sense, eight years of evidence on how that trade-off actually played out.

The post-implementation literature has grown into a genuinely large body of work — a 2023 bibliometric review counted over 400 Scopus-indexed publications on GST between 2017 and 2022 alone — but it skews heavily toward compliance-cost and revenue-collection studies, with comparatively little research on the taxpayer-concentration question this piece foregrounds. The 2019 Comptroller and Auditor General compliance audit remains one of the few official assessments to document GSTN’s early-years administrative gaps in granular detail, gaps that the filing-compliance improvement documented above (89.2% to 98.9%+) suggests have been substantially closed. On the specific question of who actually bears India’s indirect tax burden, the IMF’s periodic Selected Issues papers on India have consistently argued that GST’s multi-rate structure, imperfect as it is, does more to protect low-income consumers than a single-rate alternative would — a finding that sits somewhat in tension with the stark taxpayer-leverage numbers in this analysis, and a genuine open question for future incidence research using GSTN microdata.

References

  • Government of India, Ministry of Finance. (2015). Report on the Revenue Neutral Rate and Structure of Rates for the Goods and Services Tax. Chief Economic Advisor’s Committee (Chairman: Arvind Subramanian).
  • Comptroller and Auditor General of India. (2019). Report No. 11 of 2019: Compliance Audit — Department of Revenue: Goods and Services Tax.
  • Keen, M. (2013). The Anatomy of the VAT. National Tax Journal, 66(2), 423–446.
  • Keen, M. (2009). What Do (and Don’t) We Know About the Value Added Tax? Journal of Economic Literature, 47(1), 157–170.
  • International Monetary Fund. (2018). India: Selected Issues. IMF Country Report No. 18/255.

  • Ministry of Finance, Government of India — monthly GST collection press releases, April 2018–February 2026.
